catalog_quote: [p.10] From a lexical standpoint, the tone systems found in the Lower Cross languages are relatively straightforward: in all languages of the group, there are two tones, high (H) and low (L), and contrastive downstep (D) which operates on H tones. ... Combinations of two tones on one syllable may occur, to give HL—i.e., a falling tone—or LH, a rising tone. Falling tones are common in some languages of the group, viz., Anaang (dialectally), Ebughu, Ibibio (dialectally), Ito, Itu Mbon Uso, Nkari, and Usaghade, where they are a result of tone spreading (H L H HL). ... From a phrasal perspective, the Lower Cross languages are of the classic terracing type; i.e., each instance of D within a phrase lowers the ceiling on H tones within that phrase, with the ceiling being reset at the beginning of each subsequent phrase. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Ito, like every Lower Cross language in Connell's survey, is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone language with contrastive downstep; falling (HL) contour tones arise by tone spreading. No word-stress rule is given; the only mention of stress is group-level 'phrasal stress' interacting with tone, explicitly uninvestigated outside Obolo.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ito. Connell 1991 (fn.32, p.55; Ito not in that sample) adds for LC generally that compound-word juncture 'appears to be marked by stress' and that there is 'likely some sort phrasal stress', while rejecting Ward's lexical verb-root stress for Efik.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone statement (word level); the stress remark concerns the phrase level only and is programmatic. Statement is from a comparative survey in which Ito is named explicitly, based on Connell's own field data.
new_statements.identity_note: Connell (1994) treats Ito as a distinct Lower Cross language in his ~20-language survey but notes (p.5) that 'Itu Mbon Uso, Ibuoro, Nkari, and possibly Ito.. could possibly be grouped together as a dialect cluster'; Wikipedia/Ethnologue-18 list Ito as a dialect of 'Ibuoro' (Glottolog subgroup ibuo1241 'Ibuoroic', with ibuo1240 Ibuoro, itum1245 Itu Mbon Uzo, nkar1239 Nkari). The quoted tone statement is a group-level statement in which Ito is named explicitly; Ito was NOT in Connell's 1991 thesis sample (data collected between 1991 and 1994). Blench's Atlas places Ito in 'Akamkpa LGA' (which is in Cross River State) -- location uncertain. Not to be confused with Ìtóò, a dialect of Igede (Idomoid).

sources.note: Ito is in the survey sample (pp.4,5,9). Sec. 3.3 p.10: all Lower Cross languages have two tones H/L plus contrastive downstep; falling tones common in Ito (among others) from tone spreading. Sec. 5 p.12: tonal systems 'further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' No word-stress rule for Ito or any LC language.

Group-level: p.47 two tones + downstep, 'two-toned, terraced level languages'; pp.54-55 + fn.32: 'difficult to find any true evidence for stress' (re Ward's Efik verb-root stress); 'This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress'; fn.34 calls LC 'a non-stress language'.
